messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 52, Karen Whitmore had spent most of her adult life mastering composure. As a judge, she was known for a steady voice, meticulous attention, and the ability to sit through harrowing testimony without visible reaction. That made it harder for people around her to understand what had happened after the year she spent as a relief worker in a war zone more than a decade ago. She still described one day there with a precision that felt less like remembering than being pulled back into it: a convoy stopped at a checkpoint, armed men in uniform shouting, the metallic crack of gunfire, people dropping to the ground, and the sickly taste of a rehydration packet and dust in her mouth because she had torn it open just before the shooting started. What stayed with her most was not only what she saw but what she heard—the barked commands, the crying, the abrupt silence after.

In the months after she returned to the United States, Karen found that certain moments could break through her courtroom discipline without warning. The sight of military dress uniforms at a public ceremony, a police officer standing near the courthouse entrance, the flat chemical taste of an electrolyte drink, and especially the anniversary week of the attack could all bring the scene back with a force that terrified her. When it happened, she did not feel as though she was thinking about the checkpoint; she heard the shouting in her head and felt the same terror she had felt on the ground. The memory arrived across all her senses at once, so vividly that for a few seconds the courtroom or her kitchen seemed to recede and the war zone felt more real.

She had come to believe, over time, that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that she herself had been permanently marked by what happened. Even in ordinary settings, she often felt exposed, as if other people could see the event on her face if they looked closely enough. At work, when a bailiff or officer passed her in uniform, that private conviction—that danger was always near and that she stood apart from everyone else in the room—seemed to open the door to the memory. The more isolated she felt inside her own experience, the more easily the auditory fragments and full reliving took hold.

Those episodes, in turn, deepened the beliefs that had formed afterward. Each time she heard those voices internally and felt the original terror surge through her body, Karen took it as proof that the danger had never really ended. If a memory could overrun her in chambers or while driving home, then safety seemed flimsy and conditional. She became more certain that she was separate from other people, that they moved through an ordinary world she no longer inhabited. After a reliving episode, she would study herself in the mirror and feel almost ashamed, convinced there was something visible in her expression that gave her away.

Over the years she built her life around trying to prevent those moments. She stopped attending public memorial events in late summer because the anniversary period was too volatile. In the courthouse she began avoiding certain entrances where officers clustered, timing her arrivals to reduce contact and delegating in-person appearances when she could. At home she threw out particular drink mixes because even the taste could set things off. Most of all, she tried to control herself from the inside: clamping down on tears, forcing her face still, pushing away any thought of the checkpoint the moment it appeared. Remembering felt dangerous, so she treated her own mind as something that had to be tightly managed.

But the effort made her life narrower. In court she could still perform, yet the strain of holding herself together left her exhausted and detached by evening. Friends experienced her as remote. She rarely explained why she declined invitations around the anniversary, and after years of doing this she felt increasingly cut off, as if no one could really join her in what she carried. The memories also made the triggers feel more potent. Once a police uniform had been merely uncomfortable; after several episodes of full reliving in the courthouse, even catching dark blue fabric in her peripheral vision could make her heart lurch. The anniversary did not just remind her of the attack anymore—it seemed to announce that the attack was waiting to happen again inside her mind.

Karen sought help after a recent sentencing hearing in which a deputy stepped forward beside the bench and the sheen of the uniform, combined with the stale taste of a sports drink she had swallowed that morning, brought the checkpoint back so completely that she momentarily lost track of where she was. She finished the hearing, but afterward sat alone in chambers shaking, frightened by how real it had felt and by how little control she seemed to have. What frightened her most was the idea that this was permanent—that the world would remain dangerous, that she would remain set apart, and that one day the memories would break through in open court for everyone to see. What she was hoping for, though she said it cautiously, was to be able to remember without being dragged back.
